primitives.name: Defensive territory-minimization invariant: shrink the advance-feasible region at the snap so eleven fixed defenders can protect it; close the line rather than let it pull open
primitives.verbatim_quote: The smaller the territory is made through which an advance is possible, the better that ter- ritory may be protected by the eleven men.
primitives.latex: Source prints prose coaching doctrine with zero equations anywhere in the file; the LaTeX is a faithful predicate-logic / qualitative formalization of the printed decision rule, explicitly labeled as a formalization, not a source equation. \forall T_1,T_2:\ |T_1|<|T_2|\Rightarrow \mathrm{Protect}(11,T_1)\succ\mathrm{Protect}(11,T_2),\quad \mathrm{CloseLine}:\ |T_{after}|\le |T_{before}|,\quad n=11
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: T = set of field points through which the offense may advance [region, yd^2]; |T| = territorial measure of that feasible-advance region [yd^2]; n = 11 defenders [count, dimensionless, printed]; Protect(n,T) = qualitative protection ordering, succ = strictly better protected [ordinal, dimensionless]; CloseLine = active line-closing operator applied at the snap [0/1 action]; T_before/T_after = feasible region before/after closing [yd^2]. No printed numeric formula; ordering formalizes 'the smaller the territory ... the better that territory may be protected'.
primitives.assumptions: Eleven defenders fixed (printed 'The number of men is eleven'); defenders concentrate more quickly on a smaller region (printed 'They can concentrate more quickly upon any point attacked'); the rush line naturally pulls open on break-through (printed Diagram 14), so closing is deliberate effort not default; field width 160 feet constant (printed).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when the offense spreads the advance across the full 160-foot width faster than the line can close, so |T| cannot be reduced; mass and momentum plays (printed as largely abolished by rule) enlarge the feasible region; against a vastly superior opposing line the CloseLine operator is overpowered and territory expands despite intent.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to set-cover / facility-location concentration: with a fixed resource count n, covering a smaller feasible region T raises coverage density n/|T| and lowers response time to any attacked point. The printed line-closing rule is the defensive instantiation of minimizing the covered set's measure to maximize protection per defender.
layer2.telemetry: coverage density n/|T|; concentration time to attacked point; feasible-region measure |T| before vs after snap; line-gap width.

primitives.name: End-rush lead-intercept rule: take the sharp inward path B D, not the sideline-retreat A B, to reach the runner before interference forms and turn him into the forward pocket
primitives.verbatim_quote: The end should take direction B D, in- stead of A B or the dotted lines. He should go in on as sharp an angle and as quickly as possible,
primitives.latex: Source prints prose coaching doctrine with zero equations anywhere in the file; the LaTeX is a faithful predicate-logic / qualitative formalization of the printed decision rule, explicitly labeled as a formalization, not a source equation. \pi^{*}=\arg\min_{\pi\in\{BD,AB\}} t_{int}(\pi),\quad \mathrm{Require}\ t_{int}(\pi^{*})<t_{form},\quad \mathrm{TurnInward}(\mathrm{runner})\Rightarrow \mathrm{Pocket}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: pi = pursuit-path label {BD = sharp inward angle, AB = retreat toward side line} [categorical]; t_int(pi) = time for the end to reach the runner along path pi [s]; t_form = time for the offense to form interference [s]; TurnInward = forcing the runner toward the centre or back toward his own goal [0/1]; Pocket = stone-wall region formed by the other forwards [region]. No printed numeric formula; argmin formalizes 'go in on as sharp an angle and as quickly as possible ... reach the runner before the interference is formed'.
primitives.assumptions: The opposing end seldom or never plays in front of him (printed), so the inward path B D is available; the end keeps a little to the outside (printed); the other forwards form the pocket or stone-wall (printed 'The end drives the runner into the pocket'); end is primarily responsible for outside, secondarily inside (printed).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when interference forms before t_int (a slow end or fast formation), letting the runner get outside; over-pursuit inside abandons the primary outside responsibility; if the runner reverses toward his own goal to get around outside, the half-back must cover the vacated flank (printed).

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to pursuit / lead-collision interception geometry: choose the lead-intercept path that minimizes time-to-target and beats the target's support-formation time, rather than a trailing pure-pursuit path. The printed B D vs A B choice is the football instantiation of selecting the intercept vector that arrives before the target's protection consolidates.
layer2.telemetry: t_int vs t_form margin; inward-turn success rate; runner yards after contact; outside-contain breach rate.

primitives.name: Field-position-over-possession doctrine: prefer the opponent holding the ball at their own twenty-five to holding it yourself at your own twenty-five; kick for territory, then regain nearer their goal
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is better to allow the opposing team to have the ball on their own twenty-five- yard line than to have it yourself on your own twenty-five-yard line.
primitives.latex: Source prints prose coaching doctrine with zero equations anywhere in the file; the LaTeX is a faithful predicate-logic / qualitative formalization of the printed decision rule, explicitly labeled as a formalization, not a source equation. V(\mathrm{ball},x)\ \text{increasing in}\ x\ (\text{toward opponent goal}),\quad V(\mathrm{opp},x_{opp25})\succ V(\mathrm{self},x_{self25}),\quad \mathrm{Kick}\Rightarrow \Delta x>0\ \text{then regain}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: x = field-position coordinate measured toward the opponent goal [yd]; V(holder,x) = qualitative value of possession to a side, succ = strictly preferred [ordinal, dimensionless]; x_opp25 / x_self25 = the printed twenty-five-yard lines [yd]; Kick = territorial-advance operator [yd gained]; Delta x = net field-position gain [yd]. No printed numeric formula; ordering formalizes 'It is better to allow the opposing team to have the ball on their own twenty-five-yard line than to have it yourself on your own twenty-five-yard line'.
primitives.assumptions: Teams anywhere nearly equally matched (printed); a rushing drive exhausts strength and ammunition before reaching scoring distance (printed 'It uses up all its ammunition'); the defensive team grows stronger and the offensive weaker as the drive advances (printed); goal-to-goal rushing without relinquishing the ball is almost impossible (printed).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails for a superior mismatch that can reliably rush goal-to-goal, voiding the kick-for-territory premise; inside the opponent twenty-five, retaining possession and trying a drop dominates kicking (printed); when wind is dead against and the kicker cannot punt low into it, a slow rushing game replaces the kicking scheme (printed).

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to expected-field-position / territorial-advantage valuation: possession value is a monotone function of field position rather than a binary own/not-own state, so surrendering the ball deep in opponent territory can dominate retaining it deep in your own. The printed doctrine is the 1896 statement of position-dependent possession value.
layer2.telemetry: net field-position gain Delta x per kick; ball-regain probability; drive start field position; points per drive.

primitives.name: Kick-timing unpredictability rule: do not reserve the kick for the forced third down, where the opponent must expect it; distribute kicks across earlier downs by field zone
primitives.verbatim_quote: Do not wait until the third down to kick. Your opponent expects you to kick then, because you must.
primitives.latex: Source prints prose coaching doctrine with zero equations anywhere in the file; the LaTeX is a faithful predicate-logic / qualitative formalization of the printed decision rule, explicitly labeled as a formalization, not a source equation. P(\mathrm{kick}\mid d=3)\approx 1\Rightarrow \mathrm{Anticipated},\quad \mathrm{Spread}\ P(\mathrm{kick}\mid d)\ \text{over}\ d\in\{1,2\}\ \text{by zone},\quad \mathrm{Unpredictable}\Rightarrow \mathrm{BlockRisk}\downarrow
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: d = down index {1,2,3,4} [categorical]; P(kick|d) = conditional probability of kicking on down d [0/1, dimensionless]; Anticipated = opponent pre-reads the kick [0/1]; BlockRisk = qualitative kick-block / return risk [ordinal, dimensionless]; zone = field-position band governing the printed kick schedule [categorical]. No printed numeric formula; implication formalizes 'Your opponent expects you to kick then, because you must'.
primitives.assumptions: Printed zone schedule (first down from own ten to own forty; second down to opponent forty; third down to opponent goal); wind favorable and kickers nearly equal (printed); on third down the kick is forced so the opponent can concentrate on blocking / returning it (printed).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when wind is dead against or the kicker is inferior, forcing a rushing game (printed); when ground-gaining is easy and touchdown chance is better, retaining the ball dominates kicking (printed); a predictable early-kick tendency itself becomes exploitable if not varied.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to mixed-strategy unpredictability / predictability exploitation: a forced action on a known down is a pure strategy the opponent best-responds to, so randomizing the action's timing across downs removes the exploitable tell. The printed 'do not wait until the third down' is the football instantiation of denying the opponent a deterministic best response.
layer2.telemetry: kick-down distribution P(kick|d); kick-block rate; return yards allowed; opponent pre-snap alignment shift.

primitives.name: Loss-minimization concession kernel: when rushers are on the full-back before he can kick, concede a safety rather than risk a touchdown; better give up two points than four or six
primitives.verbatim_quote: if the opposing forwards are through the line and on him before he can get in his kick, he should allow a safety, and not give the other side a touch-down. Better give up two points than four or six.
primitives.latex: Source prints prose coaching doctrine with zero equations anywhere in the file; the LaTeX is a faithful predicate-logic / qualitative formalization of the printed decision rule, explicitly labeled as a formalization, not a source equation. a^{*}=\arg\min_{a\in\{\mathrm{safety},\mathrm{risk\ kick}\}} \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{pts\ conceded}\mid a],\quad \mathrm{safety}=2,\quad \mathrm{td}\in\{4,6\},\quad \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{pts}\mid\mathrm{risk\ kick}]\ge 2
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: a = full-back decision {concede safety, risk kick} [categorical]; pts conceded = points yielded to the opponent [points, 1896 scoring]; safety = 2 [printed points]; td in {4,6} [printed points, 1896 touchdown valuation]; E[pts|a] = expected points conceded under decision a over block / return outcomes [points]. Constants 2, 4, 6 are the printed 1896 scoring values ('Better give up two points than four or six'), not modern scoring; the argmin is a derived expected-points-loss kernel, labeled as formalization.
primitives.assumptions: Printed 1896 scoring (safety two points; touchdown four or six); opposing forwards already through the line and on the full-back before he can get in his kick (printed condition); full-back in close proximity to his own goal line (printed).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when the full-back can get the kick away safely, in which case risking it dominates conceding two; under modern scoring (safety 2, touchdown 6 with extra-point variants) the numeric arithmetic changes though the loss-minimization structure persists; if a blocked kick would not reach the goal the concession is unnecessary.

layer2.mapping: Derived expected-points-loss minimization / risk-dominant concession kernel: choose the action minimizing expected points conceded, conceding a bounded certain loss (safety = 2) to avoid a larger stochastic loss (blocked kick returned for a touchdown). The printed 'better two than four or six' is the qualitative seed of a min-expected-loss decision rule.
layer2.telemetry: E[pts|safety] = 2 vs E[pts|risk kick]; kick-block probability; safety-concession frequency; points conceded per red-zone possession.

primitives.name: Centre shortest-path rule: the straight line through the centre is the shortest distance to the required five yards, the base of a right triangle being shorter than the hypotenuse of an end run
primitives.verbatim_quote: The line through the centre* is a straight line, and therefore the shortest distance to the required five yards, as will be seen from Diagram 4, the base of a right-angled triangle being always shorter than the hypothenuse.
primitives.latex: Source prints prose coaching doctrine with zero equations anywhere in the file; the LaTeX is a faithful predicate-logic / qualitative formalization of the printed decision rule, explicitly labeled as a formalization, not a source equation. d_{centre}=b,\quad d_{end}=h,\quad b^{2}+a^{2}=h^{2}\Rightarrow b<h,\quad g=5\ \mathrm{yd},\quad \arg\min_{path} d=\mathrm{centre}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: b = straight centre-path distance (base of the right triangle) [yd]; a = lateral offset of an end run [yd]; h = end-run path distance (hypotenuse) [yd]; g = 5 required gain [printed yd]; d_path = distance to the required-distance line along a path [yd]. The Pythagorean relation is the standard mathematical expression of the printed prose 'the base of a right-angled triangle being always shorter than the hypothenuse' (Diagram 4); labeled as formalization of printed geometric prose, not a printed equation.
primitives.assumptions: Printed right-triangle geometry (Diagram 4); required distance five yards (printed); the centre hole can be forced (printed 'if you can force the centre'); forcing the centre demoralizes the opponent more than an occasional long end run (printed).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when the centre is a stone-wall (printed 'hard to gain through a good centre'), so the geometrically shortest path is blocked and a longer open path yields more; a pile-up in the hole negates the distance advantage; the shortest path is not the highest-gain path when the defence over-concentrates inside.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to Euclidean shortest-path / triangle inequality: the straight segment to a target line minimizes distance, and any lateral detour forms a hypotenuse strictly longer than the base. The printed centre-vs-end comparison is the football instantiation of the triangle inequality applied to reaching a required-distance line.
layer2.telemetry: path length b vs h; yards gained per centre attempt; required-distance conversion rate; centre-hole success probability.

reasoning_traces.think: Begin with the defensive resource-allocation problem Lewis states plainly: a fixed territory to defend and a fixed number of men, eleven, to do it with. The printed invariant is that the smaller the feasible-advance region, the better eleven men can protect it, because they can concentrate more quickly on any attacked point. This is not a numeric law but an ordering claim about coverage density, and it is the spine of the whole defensive chapter. The natural failure mode is that the rush line pulls open the instant a play starts, because each man tries to break through on the outside of his opponent; that widening enlarges the very territory the defence must cover and so weakens it. The corrective operator is therefore active line-closing at the snap, shrinking the feasible region rather than letting it expand. From this single ordering primitive the end-rush rule follows as a corollary: the end must not retreat to the side line and abandon a huge interior region to tackle and guard; he must take the sharp inward path B D so as to reach the runner before interference forms and turn him into the pocket the other forwards create. The pursuit rule is the dynamic enforcement of the static territory-minimization invariant. What is sovereign here is that Lewis derives geometry of coverage from a resource count, not from athletic heroics: eleven men protect a small region better than a large one, and every position's direction is chosen to keep the region small. The isomorphism to set-cover concentration is exact in structure, and the telemetry that would falsify it is coverage density and concentration time, not tackles counted. The deeper point is that the invariant is stated as a comparison between two regions A and B rather than as a formula, which is exactly why it survives the rule changes that abolished mass play: a coverage ordering does not depend on the particular play being stopped, only on the measure of the region the offence may advance through. That abstraction is what lets a single primitive govern the start-off defence, the scrimmage defence, and the special-play defences alike, and it is the mark of a sovereign principle rather than a situational tip.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This territory-minimization doctrine descends from the 1890s mass-momentum era, when flying wedges and push plays forced defences to think in terms of region rather than man. Lewis writes just after the rules abolished momentum and mass plays, so he inherits a defensive vocabulary built to stop concentrated force and repurposes it for a more open game. The genealogy runs from stopping a wedge by shoving its apex in and falling flat, to the general principle that a compact line resists better than a spread one. The later abolition of mass play is the retrocausal cause that lets the principle generalize from special defences to a universal coverage ordering.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Lewis models the opponent as an adaptive agent who will reinforce any known weakness, so the nominally weakest point may become the strongest. He therefore warns against the brutal policy of attacking one point until it gives way, and advises trying the whole line occasionally to catch the strong man off guard. On defence he assumes the offense will try to enlarge the feasible region by pulling the line open, and he credits the runner with trying to get outside the end. The mental model is of a thinking opponent who best-responds to predictability, which is why both the coverage invariant and the kick-timing rule are framed as denying the opponent a free read.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The coverage ordering vetoes any primitive that celebrates individual brilliance over region control: a brilliant tackle that leaves the line spread open is rejected because it enlarges the feasible territory. It also vetoes the end-rush retreat to the side line, since that abandons interior region to others. The veto is structural, not statistical: even a high tackle count fails if coverage density falls. Conversely the pursuit primitive is admitted only because it shrinks the region by turning the runner inward before interference consolidates, so the two layers reinforce rather than contradict.

reasoning_traces.think: Turn to the offensive economics of possession. Lewis's central claim is that possession value is a function of field position, not a binary state: it is better for the opponent to hold the ball at their own twenty-five than for you to hold it at yours. The reason is a drive-fatigue argument printed explicitly: a rushing team uses up its ammunition, strength, and power before it comes within scoring distance, while the defensive team grows stronger all the time. Goal-to-goal rushing without relinquishing the ball is almost impossible between nearly equal teams. Therefore the kicking game is the easiest method of gaining ground even though it surrenders the ball, because it boots the ball deep into opponent territory and then lets you wrest it back nearer their goal, where the supreme scoring effort is cheaper. This is a territorial-advantage valuation, and it is sovereign because it subordinates the naive objective of keeping the ball to the deeper objective of field position. The kick-timing rule is the game-theoretic enforcement of the same economics: if you reserve the kick for the forced third down, the opponent must expect it and can concentrate on blocking or returning it, so you distribute kicks across earlier downs by field zone to remain unpredictable. The mixed-strategy reading is exact: a forced action on a known down is a pure strategy the opponent best-responds to. The loss-minimization kernel at the other extreme, conceding a safety rather than risking a touchdown, is the same expected-value calculus applied to points conceded instead of points gained: better a bounded certain loss of two than a stochastic loss of four or six. Together these three primitives form a coherent expected-value doctrine spanning territory, timing, and risk.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The kicking-game economics is credited by Lewis to Marshall Newell and the Cornell team two seasons prior, which demonstrated the true value of kicking as part of the offence. Before that, teams kicked long but treated it as relief rather than advance. The genealogy is a shift from a rushing-only objective to a territorial objective, caused by observing that inferior teams held big teams to small scores through good full-back play and kicking. The 1896 scoring values, safety two and touchdown four or six, are the historical substrate that makes the concession kernel read differently from a modern one, and must be preserved as printed rather than normalized.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Lewis assumes the opponent is a rational anticipator: on third down the opponent expects the kick because you must kick, so he prepares to block or return it. The kick-timing rule is written against that anticipating mind, distributing kicks to deny a free read. He also models the opponent's kicker relative to your own: if their full-back is better, you rush the difference in the kicks and then boot, offsetting their superiority. The concession kernel models the opponent as ready to convert a blocked kick into a touchdown, so the full-back chooses the bounded loss. Every offensive rule is framed as a response to a thinking, best-responding opponent rather than a passive one.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The expected-value layer vetoes any primitive that treats possession as intrinsically good: keeping the ball deep in your own territory is rejected when kicking would yield better field position. It vetoes the predictable third-down-only kick because the opponent's best response erodes its value. It also vetoes risking a kick when a bounded safety concession dominates in expected points. The veto is consistent across territory, timing, and risk because all three are governed by the same expectation calculus; a primitive that maximizes a proxy such as time-of-possession while losing field position is structurally rejected.

reasoning_traces.think: Finally examine the execution-versus-formation doctrine and the geometric shortest-path claim, which together discipline how the preceding economics is implemented. Lewis insists that simple straight football should form the basis of the offence because it is more easily executed and less exhausting on body and mind, while a trick requires so many simultaneous individual actions that it produces mental strain, worry, and despair when it fails. The repertoire should be not less than twenty nor more than thirty plays, with only three or four or half a dozen tricks at most, because a few plays well executed beat a load of stuff indifferently learned. Formation may be something, but execution is everything. This is a capacity-versus-reliability tradeoff: adding plays raises nominal variety but lowers execution quality and raises mental load, so the optimum is a bounded repertoire mastered to second nature. The shortest-path primitive is the geometric counterpart applied to a single play: the straight line through the centre is the shortest distance to the required five yards, the base of a right triangle being shorter than the hypotenuse of an end run, so forcing the centre is the distance-minimizing choice and demoralizes the opponent more than an occasional long run. Yet Lewis immediately bounds this geometric truth with a breakdown regime: it is hard to gain through a good centre, so the shortest path is not always the highest-gain path. The sovereign lesson is that a clean structural principle, whether coverage density, expected value, repertoire capacity, or Euclidean distance, is always paired with the regime where it fails, and that pairing is what makes the doctrine scientific rather than dogmatic. The training chapter closes the loop: signals must be second nature with no conscious effort of memory, because team play is impossible without concert of action, and execution is everything.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The execution-over-formation doctrine reacts against the recent marvel of strategic trick play, whose growth Lewis notes was followed by a strong tendency back toward straight football. The criss-cross, the Deland momentum plays, and the Stagg concealed-ball play are the historical tricks that taught the lesson: a fine trick that fails drains the spirit needed for hard straight football. The shortest-path claim inherits elementary geometry applied to the gridiron through Diagram 4, and the training schedule inherits the old-school Herculean discipline debate, which Lewis resolves toward a happy medium allied to the old system because intermediate matches are as demanding as the final one.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Lewis models his own players as boundedly rational agents under mental strain: a trick makes them worry and wonder whether it will succeed, and failure breeds despair, so the repertoire is bounded to protect their confidence and execution. He models the opponent as someone who cannot be tricked into defeat but must be whipped into defeat, so formation is subordinate to execution. The signals must be second nature because conscious memory effort destroys concert of action. The captain must command by example rather than precept, and must not interfere with the quarter oftener than necessary, lest he make him halting and diffident. The mental model is of a team whose performance is limited by cognitive load and morale, not by schematic cleverness.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The execution layer vetoes any primitive that inflates nominal variety at the cost of reliability: a repertoire beyond thirty plays or more than half a dozen tricks is rejected because execution quality falls. It vetoes treating the geometrically shortest centre path as universally optimal, since a good centre blocks it; the shortest-path primitive is admitted only with its breakdown regime attached. It also vetoes conscious-memory signal systems, because they break concert of action. The veto binds the economic and geometric primitives to the human execution constraint, so no structurally clean rule is admitted without the regime and the cognitive load under which it actually runs.

universal_lens: Across domains the primer is a study of resource allocation under a thinking opponent: fixed defenders covering a feasible region, possession valued by field position rather than by ownership, action timing randomized to deny a best response, bounded certain loss preferred to stochastic ruin, and a bounded repertoire mastered to automaticity. These are universal decision principles, coverage density, expected value, mixed strategy, loss minimization, and capacity-reliability tradeoff, expressed in 1896 football prose with zero equations, and they transfer wherever scarce resources meet an adaptive adversary.
gsi_mapping: For the General Sovereignty Institute the primer supplies sovereign decision kernels: a coverage-density invariant for fixed-resource defense, a position-dependent possession-value ordering, a predictability-denial timing rule, a min-expected-loss concession kernel, and a Euclidean shortest-path rule with an explicit breakdown regime. Each is extracted as a labeled predicate-logic formalization of printed prose, never a fabricated equation, preserving the 1896 scoring constants verbatim and pairing every structural principle with the regime where it fails, which is the institute's standard for scientific rather than dogmatic doctrine.
